lesson.title: Fair for everyone
lesson.subtitle: Test every group, and fix bias at its source

video.title: Fair for everyone
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — your computer studies teacher, Kenya (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: A model that failed the girls
Fix it, and why it matters

scenes.visual: The computer lab. A laptop shows ‘90% right’ and the class cheers. Then Mr Joseph scrolls down a list of the model’s mistakes: almost every one has a small ‘girl’s voice’ tag. The room goes quiet; Joseph looks thoughtful.
scenes.animation: The 90% pops with confetti (0.8 s); then the mistake rows slide in and their tags light up one by one.
scenes.narration: My class trained a model to understand spoken numbers, and it scored ninety per cent. We cheered! Then we looked closer: most of its mistakes were on girls’ voices.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the course name, the lesson title and a yellow ‘AI’ track chip with the spark icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how to make your model fair for everyone it judges.

scenes.visual: A bar chart builds: ‘overall’ at 90, then it splits into two bars, ‘boys’ at 97 and ‘girls’ at 70. A thin line shows how the big pile of boys’ recordings pulls the overall bar up.
scenes.animation: The overall bar grows (600 ms), then splits into two with a small wobble.
scenes.on_screen_text: One score can hide a gap
scenes.narration: One overall score can hide a problem. Most recordings were boys’ voices, and the model got almost all of those right. On girls’ voices, it got about seven in ten. Mixed together, that still looked like ninety per cent.

scenes.visual: The test examples sort themselves into labelled trays: boys and girls, young and old, one accent and another. Each tray gets its own small score card with ticks and crosses; one card comes out much lower and glows red.
scenes.animation: Examples slide into trays (100 ms each); score cards flip over one by one.
scenes.narration: So test each group on its own. Split your test examples by group: boys and girls, young and old, one accent and another. Count right and wrong for each. If one group scores much lower, your model is failing them.

scenes.visual: Clean white card with the AI track chip. The word ‘bias’ appears. Below it, the class’s pile of recordings: four microphone icons in a row, three marked ‘boy’, one marked ‘girl’.
scenes.animation: Microphone icons pop in one by one (200 ms); the ‘3 in 4’ count grows.
scenes.narration: When a model makes more mistakes for one group than for others, it’s biased. Bias usually starts in the data: a group that’s missing, or too small. In Mr Joseph’s class, three in four recordings were boys’.

scenes.visual: A tailor’s stall at the market. The tailor measures one customer and sews: the shirt fits him perfectly. A line of other customers tries on the same shirt: sleeves too short, too long, too tight. The tailor scratches his head, tape measure still around his neck.
scenes.animation: The tape measure unrolls (300 ms); each new customer pops in with a small bounce.
scenes.on_screen_text: Like a tailor with one customer
scenes.narration: It’s like a tailor who learned from one person’s measurements. Every shirt fits that person perfectly. On everyone else, the sleeves are too short! The tailor isn’t unkind; they never measured anyone else.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma beside a big ‘95%’ score card for a leaf-disease model, arms folded, one eyebrow raised. Three answer cards drop in below her.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A leaf-disease model scores ninety-five per cent overall. What should you check next?

scenes.visual: The card ‘Its score for each region’ gets a blue check badge. A map splits into regions, each with its own score; one region’s score is far lower and pulses.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms). Regions fill in one by one; the low score pulses twice.
scenes.narration: Its score for each region, or each group it serves. A great overall score can hide a group the model fails badly. So test groups separately, every time.

scenes.visual: Back in Mr Joseph’s class: girls record their numbers into a phone, after a nod of agreement. New labelled recordings join the pile, the model retrains, and the boys’ and girls’ bars rise to nearly the same height.
scenes.animation: Recordings drop into the pile (150 ms each); the cog turns; the girls’ bar grows (800 ms).
scenes.narration: So how do you fix bias? Go back to the data. Collect examples from the missing group, with permission, and label them carefully. Then train again and test every group. When the girls in Mr Joseph’s class recorded their numbers, the gap almost closed.

scenes.visual: Three cards, about 5 seconds each: a farmer in the hills looking at a phone that says ‘healthy’ over a sick plant; an older woman speaking into a phone that shows a jumble of wrong words; then a wide shot of many different people, each getting a correct result.
scenes.animation: Each card flips in from the side; the last one fans out into many small figures.
scenes.narration: Why does this matter? Because models judge real people. A leaf spotter that fails hill farmers can cost them a harvest. A voice tool that can’t hear an accent shuts people out. Fair means it works for everyone it judges, not just those in its data.

scenes.visual: A phone screen showing the ‘Bias in data’ lab: a chart of leaf photos from the sunny valley and the cloudy hills, a dashed line where the model switches from healthy to sick, and four bars: wrong overall, wrong in the valley, wrong in the hills, sick leaves missed in the hills. A slider for hill photos moves up and the hill bars shrink.
scenes.animation: The slider moves (1 s); the dashed line tilts; the bars shrink.
scenes.narration: In the app, a leaf-disease spotter learned mostly from sunny-valley photos, but hill photos come out darker. Its overall score looks great, yet it misses about a third of sick leaves in the hills. Add hill photos, and watch the gap close.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph beside a phone showing a voice model’s results: good for young voices, poor for older ones. Three answer cards appear beside him.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Your voice model struggles with older people’s voices. What’s the best fix?

scenes.visual: The ‘Record more older voices’ card gets the check badge, then the screen resolves into four summary lines and a closing line.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in one by one, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Record more older voices, with permission, then test every group again. Remember: one overall score can hide a group the model fails. Test each group separately. Fix bias at its source, the data, so the model works for everyone.

scenes.visual: A family at home in the evening: a grandmother, a parent and a younger cousin each say the same sentence into a phone’s voice typing while a student ticks the words it got right in a notebook. Mr Joseph gives a thumbs up. End card: the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Words appear on the phone one by one; ticks and crosses pop in the notebook. End card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: test voice typing or a translator with your family: young and old, different accents or languages. Ask first, then have each person say the same three sentences. Count the words it gets right. Who does it understand best, and why?

checkpoints.prompt: A leaf-disease model scores 95% overall. What should you check next?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — an overall score can hide a region where it fails. Check each group separately.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — training photos can’t show fairness, and 95% overall can hide a group it fails. Check each region’s score.

checkpoints.prompt: Your voice model struggles with older people’s voices. What’s the best fix?

options.text: Record more older voices, with permission
Ask older people to speak differently

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — fix it at the source: collect the missing voices, then test every group again.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the problem is in the data, not in how people speak, and hiding it fixes nothing. Collect the missing voices.
